newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan contractors report mixed earnings.
newsitem.headline: Japan contractors report mixed earnings.

text.p: Japan's leading contractors reported mixed half-year profits on Friday as some still suffered damage from the country's prolonged economic stagnation.
Many builders continue to be burdened by massive debts and large losses on real estate holdings as a result of the burst of the 1980s "economic bubble" of inflated asset prices.
But there are some bright signs. Kajima Corp and Obayashi Corp saw their profits grow, mainly on increased revenues from recently completed construction projects.

Kajima saw its sales in the first half of the business year increase 18.6 percent from a year ago to 659.5 billion yen ($5.94 billion), and parent current profit rise 13.9 percent to 10.3 billion yen ($92.7 million).
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities, such as investment in stocks.

Obayashi posted sales of 630.3 billion yen ($5.67 billion), up 25.9 percent from a year ago, and parent current profit of 15.2 billion yen ($136 million), up 41.7 percent in the six month to September.

"Some top-ranking builders' profitability is gradually improving as they are building more offices and fewer residential condominiums," said Noboru Mimura, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson (Asia) Ltd.
Office building projects are far more profitable than condominiums, the analyst said.
However, Shimizu Corp's half-year sales fell 5.9 percent year-on-year to 647.8 billion yen ($5.83 billion). Parent current profit was down 13.0 percent to 10.3 billion yen ($92.7 million).
Taisei Corp also saw its half-year sales decline by 1.9 percent year-on-year to 632.3 billion yen ($5.69 billion), while parent current profit fell 39.4 percent to 8.3 billion yen ($74.7 million).
"The near 40 percent fall in pre-tax profit was because many of our construction projects completed during the half year period had low profit margins," a Taisei spokesman said.
Builders have been facing small profit margins and few orders, especially from the private sector, due to Japan's sluggish economic conditions in the past several years.

Instead, the builders' earnings have been helped by public-sector orders. The Japanese government has been placing massive public works orders in the hope that they would stimulate the stagnant economy.

However, the pattern appears to be changing. All but one of the top four builders said in their interim earnings reports that orders in the first half increased from a year ago despite the fact public-sector orders declined in the first half.
The amount of orders will affect future earnings as sales are posted when the construction is completed.
However, uncertainties remain with some companies burdened by considerable interest payments on their massive debts.
The total interest-bearing debts at the top four builders stood at 2.42 trillion yen ($21.8 billion) at the end of September, down slightly from 2.52 trillion six months ago.

Falling land prices are also a concern, analysts pointed out. Construction companies hold land whose values have fallen sharply after the end of economic boom in late 1980s. The properties would incur losses if they were sold off.

Teikoku Databank Ltd said in a survey that hidden losses on real estate holdings by the nation's 72 general contractors were estimated to have grown to 1.41 trillion yen ($12.7 billion) by the end of the 1995/96 fiscal year to March 31, up 85.1 percent from a year earlier. ($1=111 yen)
